title: Program Correctness
body:
Proving that a program does what it is supposed to, rather than testing that it did on the
inputs you thought of. This is the payoff the rest of the course was setting up:
[[Pure Function|purity]] makes programs into equations, and equations can be reasoned about the
way [[DISCRETE MATH|discrete maths]] reasons about anything else.

The contrast with [[Unit testing]] is the honest framing. A test shows the function works for
one input. A proof shows it works for **all** of them, including the ones nobody thought of.
[[Unit testing]] is cheap and finds real bugs; a proof is expensive and finds the absence of
them. Dijkstra's line is the one to remember: testing shows the presence of bugs, never their
absence.

## Equational reasoning

In a pure language, `=` in a definition really is equality, so you may substitute one side for
the other anywhere, forever. That is [[Pure Function|referential transparency]] used as a proof
rule, and it is just beta reduction from [[Lambda Calculus]] promoted to a tool.

```haskell
double x  = x * 2
quad x    = double (double x)
```

$$\texttt{quad } 3 = \texttt{double (double 3)} = \texttt{double (3 * 2)} = \texttt{double 6} = 6 * 2 = 12$$

Every step replaced a subterm by an equal subterm, and no step needed to know anything about
what had happened before or what happens next. Try that with

```c
int counter = 0;
int next(void) { return ++counter; }
```

where `next() + next()` cannot be simplified at all, because the two calls are not the same
value and the order matters. **Impurity does not make the proof harder, it removes the rule the
proof was using.**

## Structural induction

Equational reasoning handles straight-line definitions. Recursive ones need induction, and the
shape of the induction is handed to you by the [[Algebraic Data Type]]: one case per
constructor, base cases for the base constructors and an inductive step for the recursive ones.

```haskell
data List a = Nil | Cons a (List a)

length' Nil          = 0
length' (Cons _ xs)  = 1 + length' xs

(++) Nil         ys = ys
(++) (Cons x xs) ys = Cons x (xs ++ ys)
```

**Claim.** `length' (xs ++ ys) = length' xs + length' ys` for all `xs`.

*Base case*, `xs = Nil`:

```
length' (Nil ++ ys)  =  length' ys              (definition of ++)
                     =  0 + length' ys          (arithmetic)
                     =  length' Nil + length' ys  (definition of length')
```

*Inductive step*, `xs = Cons z zs`, assuming the claim for `zs`:

```
length' ((Cons z zs) ++ ys)
  = length' (Cons z (zs ++ ys))        (definition of ++)
  = 1 + length' (zs ++ ys)             (definition of length')
  = 1 + (length' zs + length' ys)      (induction hypothesis)
  = (1 + length' zs) + length' ys      (associativity)
  = length' (Cons z zs) + length' ys   (definition of length')
```

$\blacksquare$ Every line is a definition unfolded or a known law applied. That is the whole
technique, and it is available only because nothing in either function can have side effects.

## It is ordinary induction

Structural induction is [[Proof By Induction]] with the naturals replaced by a recursive type.
[[Induction]] ([[DISCRETE MATH]], MATH 1271) already draws the distinction and names the COMP places structural
induction gets used; this is the course it was pointing at.

| | Ordinary ([[Proof By Induction]]) | Structural |
|---|---|---|
| Domain | $\mathbb{N}$ | a recursive [[Algebraic Data Type]] |
| Base | $P(0)$ | one case per non-recursive constructor |
| Step | $P(n) \Rightarrow P(n+1)$ | assume for the substructures, prove for the whole |
| Why it terminates | every $n$ reachable from 0 | every finite value built from base constructors |

The two are the same theorem over a different well-founded order, and $\mathbb{N}$ is the
special case where the type is `data Nat = Zero | Succ Nat`. The well-foundedness requirement is
also why the argument only covers **finite** structures: [[Lazy Evaluation]] permits infinite
lists, and the claim above says nothing about them.

## What it does not cover

Worth stating plainly, because the technique oversells easily.

- **Only finite, total values.** Infinite structures and non-terminating definitions are outside
  the argument, and Haskell has both.
- **Termination is separate.** The proof above assumes `length'` terminates. That is an appeal
  to [[Recursion Schemes|structural recursion]] shrinking its argument, and in general it is
  [[Undecidability|undecidable]].
- **Space and time are not covered.** The `foldl` leak from [[Lazy Evaluation]] is a correct
  program by this standard and still exhausts memory.
- **The specification can be wrong.** A proof relates code to a claim, and the claim is written
  by a person.
- **Effects are not covered by these rules.** Reasoning about [[Monadic IO]] needs the
  [[Monad]] laws instead, which is what those laws are for.

## Core Facts to Know

- Testing shows bugs are present; a proof shows they are absent.
- **Equational reasoning**: substitute equals for equals, licensed by referential transparency.
- It is beta reduction from [[Lambda Calculus]] used as a proof rule.
- Impurity removes the rule rather than complicating it: `next() + next()` cannot be simplified.
- **Structural induction**: one case per constructor of the [[Algebraic Data Type]].
- The data definition determines the proof's shape, and the function's shape, identically.
- It is [[Proof By Induction]] with $\mathbb{N}$ replaced by a recursive type.
- It covers finite, total values only.
- Termination is a separate obligation and undecidable in general.
- The [[Monad]] laws are the corresponding tool for effectful code.
